title: Mosques of mud and wood
hookLine: Djenné in Mali, wooden mosques in China and Java

lines: A ROOF OF MUD IN MALI.
cards: Three roofs. The first is flat, on walls of sun-dried mud bristling with wooden poles, in Djenné, in Mali. The second curves up at the corners like a temple roof, painted beams under clay tiles, in China.
The third is stacked roof on roof, a tall wooden pyramid in Java. No dome on any of them, no pencil minaret. And all three are mosques, where people line up in rows and bow toward Mecca.
How can three buildings look so unlike each other and do the same thing? Today: mosques of mud and wood.

teach.h: THE WHOLE EARTH IS A PLACE OF PRAYER.
teach.b: The answer starts with a saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him.

In a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, he counts the things given to him, and one is this: the whole earth has been made a place of prayer for him and his community. Wherever the time of prayer finds you, you can pray there.
So a mosque, at its simplest, is a clean place set apart, with the direction of Mecca marked. The rest is left to the builders, and builders use what they have. Second, the mud.
We met Djenné earlier this year, the town that replasters its mosque together. This time, look at the method.

teach.h: MUD IN MALI, FROM THE RIVER.
teach.b: In a land of river clay and heat, thick mud walls help keep a building cool, and the wooden poles give the plasterers a foothold when the walls are renewed. Local material, local work. Third, China.

teach.h: TIMBER AND CURVED ROOFS IN CHINA.
teach.b: Some old Chinese mosques were built in the style of Chinese halls: courtyards, gates, timber, curved roofs, inscriptions in Arabic and Chinese side by side. A visitor might take one for a temple until the rows begin.

teach.h: TIERED ROOFS ON PILLARS IN JAVA.
teach.b: Some old mosques there have tiered roofs on great wooden pillars, the way halls were raised on that island. People in Demak tell of one pillar pieced together from leftover wood chips by a saintly teacher.
It's a story, not a record, but it shows how dearly the building is loved.

teach.h: NATIONS AND TRIBES THAT YE MAY KNOW ONE ANOTHER.
teach.b: The Qur'an says God made people "nations and tribes that ye may know one another." The mosques look like their nations. The rows inside look the same.

how: Muslims pray in mosques of every style and material, and when no mosque is near they pray on any clean ground or a prayer mat, facing the direction of Mecca.

o: a Javanese mosque with a tiered wooden roof
a Malian town whose mosque is built of mud

s: a mosque must have a dome and a minaret
the mosques of Djenné, China and Java show other shapes. what a mosque needs is a clean place and the direction of Mecca.
a hadith says the whole earth was made a place of prayer
the Prophet counted it among the things given to him: wherever the time of prayer finds you, pray there.
the wood-chip pillar of Demak is a recorded historical fact
it's a story people tell about a saintly teacher, not a record.

games.q: you're building a mosque on an island of heavy rain and great forests, far from any desert. what do you build it from?
o: marble shipped from far away, to look like the mosques of Arabia.
the island's own timber, under the roof shape the island knows.
games.why: old mosques of Java, like the one at Demak, were raised on great wooden pillars under tiered roofs, the way halls were built on that island.

practice: Build a mosque in your mind from what's around you, or from the place you grew up: brick, stone, timber, adobe, city concrete.
Let it rise slowly, wall by wall, and last of all give one wall a small mark for the direction of prayer, the one thing every mosque shares. If you pray, bring that house into your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Djenné, the Malian town whose mud mosque has thick walls for the heat and wooden poles that give plasterers a foothold when it's renewed. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: mosque, a place set apart for prayer.

carryVoice: Your line: every land builds its own. The roofs differ; the rows don't. Back tomorrow, same hill.
